title: Critical Reasoning & Truth-Teller Puzzles
relevance: Campus OAs and SDE screens routinely test whether candidates can isolate assumptions, strengthen or weaken causal links, and solve knights/knaves and syllogism puzzles under time pressure.

phases.goal: Establish the premise–conclusion–assumption framework and the Negation Test for required assumptions.

must_hit.point: Every argument has a premise (stated facts), a conclusion (the claim), and an assumption (the unstated link connecting them).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names all three parts and describes the assumption as the missing bridge, not a restated premise.

must_hit.point: Use the Negation Test: if negating a candidate assumption destroys the argument, that assumption is logically required.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate applies negate-and-check: destruction of the plan or claim means the assumption was necessary.

must_hit.point: To strengthen or weaken an argument, support or attack the assumption link so a new fact makes the conclusion more or less likely to follow from the evidence.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says you target the reasoning bridge, not merely restate or deny the given facts.

probes: What are the three parts of an argument, and how do you check whether a statement is a required assumption?

hints.1: Think about what is stated versus what must be true but never said.
hints.2: Name premise, conclusion, and assumption, then try flipping the assumed link and see if the argument collapses.
hints.3: Negation Test: negate the candidate assumption; if the argument is destroyed, that assumption is required. Strengthen/weaken by supporting or attacking that link.

phases.goal: Show how to solve statement–assumption, strengthen/weaken, cause–effect, knights/knaves, and syllogism problems with the right check.

must_hit.point: For a pollution-reduction plan that raises parking fees, only the assumption that people will switch to public transport or carpool is implicit; assuming people still drive despite paying more undermines the plan.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks only the deterrence/switch assumption and explains why continued driving kills the pollution goal.

must_hit.point: Weaken a causal claim (e.g., heavy breakfast caused 15% higher exam scores) by giving an alternative cause such as skippers studying late and sleeping less; strengthen a causal claim with a clear before-and-after after the claimed mechanism was introduced.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites alternative cause for weaken and before/after improvement for strengthen, not out-of-scope side facts.

must_hit.point: Solve knights/knaves by case-splitting: assume a speaker’s type; if contradiction follows, flip. No one can claim “I am a liar.”
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate tries Knight vs Knave cases and recalls that neither type can say they are a liar.

must_hit.point: For syllogisms, translate All/Some/No into Venn relations; a conclusion follows only if it holds in every valid diagram.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate draws or describes nested/overlapping/disjoint circles and rejects conclusions that are merely possible.

probes: How would you weaken a principal’s claim that a heavy breakfast caused higher exam scores, and how do you decide whether a syllogism conclusion follows?

hints.1: For cause claims, ask what else could explain the effect; for sets, ask what must be true in every diagram.
hints.2: Weaken via alternative cause; strengthen via before-and-after on the claimed mechanism; use case splits for knights/knaves and Venns for All/Some/No.
hints.3: Breakfast→scores is weakened if late studying/sleep explains low scores; All computers are machines and some machines are robots does not force any computer–robot overlap.

phases.goal: Distinguish attacking the premise or scope from attacking the reasoning link, and choose the move that actually strengthens or weakens the argument.

must_hit.point: When asked to weaken, attacking the premise (e.g., calling data fake) or picking a generally true but out-of-scope fact fails; you must attack the reasoning that connects premise to conclusion.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects premise-bashing and off-topic truths and instead breaks the causal or inferential bridge.

must_hit.point: For LED bills that rose after a switch, critics blaming hungrier bulbs are weakened by more fixtures being added; for low lost-luggage claims, direct flights or fewer bags offer rival causes that weaken a scanning-system explanation, while a worst-to-best shift after installing the system strengthens it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts alternative causes that break a causal story with before-and-after evidence that supports the claimed cause.

probes: On a weaken question, why is attacking the premise or picking an out-of-scope true fact usually wrong, and what should you attack instead?

hints.1: Separate “this fact is true” from “this fact breaks the author’s logic.”
hints.2: Premise attacks and off-topic truths leave the link intact; alternative causes or missing bridges break it.
hints.3: Weaken by hitting the assumption/causal link (more lights, sleep deprivation, Friday deadlines); strengthen by closing rival explanations or showing before-and-after on the claimed mechanism.

phases.goal: Apply the framework to OA-style assumption, weaken, inference, two-guard, and multi-statement syllogism items.

must_hit.point: If an AI assistant reduces syntax errors by 40% and the claim is that overall development time will fall, it must be true that syntax errors currently account for a significant portion of development time; otherwise the 40% cut barely moves overall time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate applies Negation Test to the significant-share assumption and rejects free deployment or faster writing as the necessary link.

must_hit.point: A 30% Thursday commit rise after a no-meetings policy is weakened if a mandatory Friday morning code-review deadline forced rushed Thursday commits.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the Friday-deadline alternative cause and dismisses morale, other companies, or bug counts as off-metric.

must_hit.point: From intermittency of solar/wind plus the need for massive battery investment for a 100% renewable grid, infer that without large-scale storage a grid relying entirely on wind and solar would be unstable—not that solar beats wind or that batteries are too expensive.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sticks to text-entailed instability without storage and rejects reliability comparisons and cost claims.

must_hit.point: In the two-door, two-guard puzzle, ask what the other guard would say is the freedom door; both types point to doom, so take the opposite door. With All anomalies are alerts, no alert is a false positive, and some false positives are user errors, both “no anomaly is a false positive” and “some user errors are not anomalies” follow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains the double-negative doom answer and the chained Venn: anomalies inside alerts, alerts disjoint from false positives, so some false-positive user errors cannot be anomalies.

probes: For the AI 40% syntax-error argument and the Thursday no-meetings 30% commit claim, what must be true or what weakens the conclusion?

hints.1: Ask what link turns a narrow metric change into the broad claimed outcome.
hints.2: Negate “syntax errors take significant time”; for commits, hunt a rival Thursday cause like a Friday deadline.
hints.3: Necessary: syntax errors are a significant time share. Weaken: Friday review deadline drives Thursday commits. Two-guards: ask what the other would say, then pick the opposite door.

tradeoffs.topic: Attacking the premise vs attacking the assumption link
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Weaken/strengthen items are decided on the reasoning bridge. Calling data fake or citing a true but out-of-scope fact leaves the argument’s link intact; a new fact must make the conclusion more or less likely given the same evidence.

tradeoffs.topic: Alternative cause vs outlier or off-scope fact when weakening causation
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A rival cause for the same effect (sleep loss instead of skipped breakfast; more fixtures instead of power-hungry LEDs; Friday deadlines instead of no-meeting deep work) breaks causation. Outliers that leave the average intact, or facts about cost, morale, lunch, or other companies, usually do not.

tradeoffs.topic: Possible Venn overlap vs necessary conclusion
tradeoffs.strong_answer: In syllogisms, a conclusion follows only if every valid diagram forces it. Some machines are robots does not force robots to meet computers inside machines; some erasers are pencils does follow from all pencils are erasers.

gotchas.trap: Picking an option that attacks the premise or is generally true but out of scope when asked to weaken.
gotchas.correction: Attack the reasoning that connects premise to conclusion—typically an alternative cause or a broken assumption link.

gotchas.trap: Treating “engineers may introduce new logical errors” as necessary to block “less syntax error → less development time.”
gotchas.correction: Even with some new errors, overall time can still fall if syntax savings are large; what is necessary is that syntax errors currently take a significant share of time.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a character can say “I am a liar,” or stopping after one case without checking contradiction.
gotchas.correction: Neither Knight nor Knave can claim to be a liar. Case-split: assume a type, derive contradiction, flip; e.g., “at least one Knave” forces A Knight and B Knave.

gotchas.trap: Accepting a syllogism conclusion that might be true in some diagrams but not all (e.g., some robots are computers from All computers are machines + Some machines are robots).
gotchas.correction: Require truth in every valid Venn; possible overlap is not enough. Conversely, all pencils are erasers does force some erasers are pencils.

gotchas.trap: Overreaching from “longer battery life” to “older phones had poor battery life,” or comparing solar vs wind reliability when the passage does not.
gotchas.correction: Only force what the text requires: other components must not wipe out battery/processor gains; without storage, a 100% wind/solar grid would be unstable.
